title: De Beneficiis
author: Lucius Annaeus Seneca
source: Translated by Claude from phi1017.phi013.perseus-lat2, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Nam praeter ista, quae Hecaton transcribit, tres Chrysippus Gratias ait Iovis et Eurynomes filias esse, aetate autem minores quam Horas, sed meliuscula facie et ideo Veneri datas comites. Matris quoque nomen ad rem iudicat pertinere : Eurynomen enim dictam, quia late patentis patrimonii sit beneficia dividere ; tamquam matri post filias soleat nomen imponi aut poetae vera nomina reddant !
passages.english: For besides the things that Hecaton copies out, Chrysippus says that the three Graces are daughters of Jupiter and Eurynome, younger in age than the Hours but somewhat prettier in looks, and for that reason given to Venus as companions. He judges that the mother's name too bears on the matter: she was called Eurynome, he says, because distributing benefits is the mark of a widely extended estate. As if a mother usually received her name after her daughters, or poets gave true names!
passages.notes: Eurynome's name is taken as Greek for 'wide-ranging' (eury- 'wide' + nomē 'distribution, pasture'); Seneca's Latin 'late patentis patrimonii' plays on this.

passages.original: Quemadmodum nomenclatori memoriae loco audacia est et, cuicumque nomen non potest reddere, imponit, ita poetae non putant ad rem pertinere verum dicere, sed aut necessitate coacti aut decore corrupti id quemque vocari iubent, quod belle facit ad versum. Nec illis fraudi est, si aliud in censum detulerunt ; proximus enim poeta suum illas ferre nomen iubet. Hoc ut scias ita esse, ecce Thalia, de qua cum maxime agitur, apud Hesiodum Charis est, apud Homerum Musa.
passages.english: Just as a nomenclator uses boldness in place of memory and, to anyone whose name he cannot give back, assigns one, so poets do not think it matters to tell the truth. Either forced by necessity or seduced by elegance, they order each person to be called whatever fits nicely in the verse. Nor is it held against them if they have entered some other name on the census roll, for the next poet orders them to bear his own name for them. So that you may know this is so, look: Thalia, who is the one especially under discussion, is a Grace in Hesiod and a Muse in Homer.
passages.notes: *nomenclator*: a slave who prompted his master with the names of people met. In the last sentence the Latin uses the Greek word 'Charis' (Grace).

passages.original: Ad hanc honestissimam contentionem beneficiis beneficia vincendi sic nos adhortatur Chrysippus, ut dicat verendum esse, ne, quia Charites Iovis filiae sunt, parum se grate gerere sacrilegium sit et tam bellis puellis fiat iniuria !
passages.english: Chrysippus urges us to this most honourable contest, of outdoing benefits with benefits, by saying that we must beware lest, since the Charites are daughters of Jupiter, behaving with too little gratitude should be sacrilege and an injury be done to such pretty girls!
passages.notes: Charites: the Greek name for the Graces.

passages.original: Socrati cum multa pro suis quisque facultatibus offerrent, Aeschines, pauper auditor: " Nihil," inquit, " dignum te, quod dare tibi possim, invenio et hoc uno modo pauperem esse me sentio. Itaque dono tibi, quod unum habeo, me ipsum. Hoc munus rogo, qualecumque est, boni consulas cogitesque alios, cum multum tibi darent, plus sibi reliquisse." Cui Socrates :
passages.english: When many people were offering Socrates gifts, each according to his means, Aeschines, a poor pupil of his, said: "I find nothing worthy of you that I could give you, and in this one way I feel that I am poor. So I give you the one thing I have: myself. I ask you to take this gift in good part, whatever it is, and to reflect that the others, though they gave you much, left more for themselves." To him Socrates [said]:
passages.notes: The passage ends mid-sentence; Socrates' reply follows in the continuation of the text.

passages.original: Qui gratus futurus est, statim, dum accipit, de reddendo cogitet. Chrysippus quidem ait illum velut in certamen cursus compositum et carceribus inclusum opperiri debere tempus suum, ad quod velut dato signo prosiliat ; et quidem magna illi contentione opus est, magna celeritate, ut consequatur antecedentem.
passages.english: The one who means to be grateful should think about repaying at once, while he is receiving. Chrysippus indeed says that he, like someone set for a race and shut in the starting gates, must wait for his moment, at which he may leap forward as if the signal had been given. And he certainly needs great effort and great speed to catch the one who is ahead.

passages.original: Servus, ut placet Chrysippo, perpetuus mercennarius est. Quemadmodum ille beneficium dat, ubi plus praestat, quam in quod operas locavit, sic servus : ubi benevolentia erga dominum fortunae suae modum transit et altius aliquid ausus, quod etiam felicius natis decori esset, spem domini antecessit, beneficium est intra domum inventum.
passages.english: A slave, as Chrysippus holds, is a hired worker for life. Just as the hired worker gives a benefit when he provides more than what he contracted his labour for, so too the slave: when his goodwill towards his master passes the limit of his condition, and, daring something loftier that would do credit even to those more fortunately born, he goes beyond his master's hopes, it is a benefit found within the household.

passages.original: Ex omnibus, quae tractavimus, Aebuti Liberalis, potest videri nihil tam necessarium aut magis, ut ait Sallustius, cum cura dicendum, quam quod in manibus est : an beneficium dare et in vicem gratiam referre per se res expetendae sint.
passages.english: Of all the matters we have dealt with, Aebutius Liberalis, nothing may seem so necessary, or more in need, as Sallust says, of being spoken of with care, than the one in hand: whether giving a benefit and returning gratitude in turn are things to be sought for their own sake.

passages.original: Non dicam pudicam, quae amatorem ut incenderet reppulit, quae aut legem aut virum timuit ; ut ait Ovidius : Quae, quia non licuit, non dedit, illa dedit. Non immerito in numerum peccantium refertur, quae pudicitiam timori praestitit, non sibi. Eodem modo, qui beneficium ut reciperet dedit, non dedit.
passages.english: I will not call a woman chaste who rebuffed a lover in order to inflame him, or who feared either the law or her husband. As Ovid says: "She who did not give because it was not allowed, gave." Not undeservedly is she counted among sinners who kept her chastity for the sake of fear, not for her own. In the same way, the one who gave a benefit in order to receive one back did not give.

passages.original: Socrates parem gratiam Archelao referre non posset, si illum regnare vetuisset ? Parum scilicet magnum beneficium a Socrate accipiebat, si ullum dare Socrati potuisset. Quare ergo hoc Socrates dixit ? Vir facetus et cuius per figuras sermo procederet, derisor omnium, maxime potentium, maluit illi nasute negare quam contumaciter aut superbe ; dixit se nolle beneficia ab eo accipere, cui non posset paria reddere.
passages.english: Could Socrates not have made an equal return to Archelaus if he had forbidden him to be king? Evidently it was too small a benefit that he was receiving from Socrates, if he could have given any to Socrates! Why then did Socrates say this? Being a witty man, whose speech proceeded by figures, a mocker of everyone, especially of the powerful, he preferred to refuse him slyly rather than defiantly or proudly; he said that he did not wish to accept benefits from a man to whom he could not return equal ones.
passages.notes: The first sentence appears to be put ironically, implying that by teaching Archelaus to renounce kingship Socrates would have more than repaid him. 'Nasute' (literally 'with a nose', i.e. with sly mockery) is rendered 'slyly'.

passages.original: Quem magis admiraberis, quam qui imperat sibi, quam qui se habet in potestate ? Gentes facilius est barbaras impatientesque arbitrii alieni regere, quam animum suum continere et tradere sibi. Platon, inquit, agit Socrati gratias, quod ab illo didicit ; quare Socrates sibi non agat, quod ipse se docuit ? M. Cato ait : ' Quod tibi deerit, a te ipso mutuare.' Quare donare mihi non possim, si commodare possum ? Innumerabilia sunt, in quibus consuetudo nos dividit ;
passages.english: Whom will you admire more than the one who rules himself, than the one who has himself in his own power? It is easier to rule barbarian nations that cannot bear the will of another than to restrain one's own mind and hand oneself over to oneself. Plato, he says, thanks Socrates because he learned from him; why should Socrates not thank himself because he taught himself? Marcus Cato says: 'Whatever you lack, borrow from yourself.' Why can I not give to myself, if I can lend [to myself]? There are countless matters in which usage divides us;
passages.notes: 'Inquit' ('he says') introduces an imagined objector or interlocutor. The passage breaks off mid-sentence.

passages.original: Cleanthes exemplo eiusmodi utitur : " Ad quaerendum," inquit, " et accersendum ex Academia Platonem duos pueros misi. Alter totam porticum perscrutatus est, alia quoque loca, in quibus illum inveniri posse sperabat, percucurrit et domum non minus lassus quam irritus redit ;
passages.english: Cleanthes uses an example of this kind: "I sent two boys," he says, "to look for Plato and fetch him from the Academy. One searched the whole portico, ran through other places too where he hoped he could be found, and comes home no less tired than unsuccessful;
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence; the second boy's conduct follows in the continuation.

passages.original: Multum enim interest, utrum aliquis beneficium nobis det sua causa an et sua. Ille, qui totus ad se spectat et nobis prodest, quia aliter prodesse sibi non potest, eo mihi loco est, quo, qui pecori suo hibernum et aestivum pabulum prospicit; eo loco est, quo, qui captivos suos, ut commodius veneant, pascit et ut opimos boves saginat ac defricat, quo lanista, qui familiam summa cura exercet atque ornat. Multum, ut ait Cleanthes, a beneficio distat negotiatio.
passages.english: For it makes a great difference whether someone gives us a benefit for his own sake, or for his own sake as well. The one who looks wholly to himself and helps us because he cannot help himself otherwise stands, in my view, in the same position as one who provides winter and summer fodder for his flock; in the same position as one who feeds his captives so that they may sell more profitably, and fattens and rubs down oxen for market; as a trainer of gladiators who exercises and equips his troupe with the greatest care. Trading, as Cleanthes says, is far removed from a benefit.
passages.notes: 'ut opimos boves saginat' read as 'fattens [them] as one does prime oxen' or 'fattens prime oxen'; the sense is similar.

passages.original: Platon cum flumen nave transisset nec ab illo quicquam portitor exegisset, honori hoc suo datum credens dixit positum illi esse apud Platonem officium; deinde paulo post, cum alium atque alium gratis eadem sedulitate transveheret, negavit illi iam apud Platonem positum officium.
passages.english: When Plato had crossed a river by boat and the ferryman had demanded nothing from him, he, believing this had been granted out of respect for him, said that the man had laid up a service to his credit with Plato. Then a little later, when [he saw] him ferrying one person after another free with the same diligence, he said that the man no longer had a service laid up with Plato.

passages.original: Socrates amicis audientibus : " Emissem," inquit, " pallium, si nummos haberem." Neminem poposcit, omnes admonuit. A quo acciperet, ambitus fuit; quidni esset ? Quantulum enim erat, quod Socrates accipiebat ! At multum erat eum fuisse, a quo Socrates acciperet.
passages.english: Socrates, in the hearing of his friends, said: "I would have bought a cloak, if I had the money." He asked no one, [but] he reminded everyone. There was competition over whom he would accept it from; and why should there not have been? For how little it was that Socrates was receiving! But it was a great thing to have been the one from whom Socrates received.
passages.notes: 'Ambitus fuit' is taken as 'there was rivalry/competition' among the friends.
